The breast cancer gene is on chromosome 17q21.  It has been identified and
cloned.  The name of the gene is BRCA1.

The gene has not been sequenced.  Once they finish sequencing it, they may
be able to make a kit that can be used to screen for it.  The way it works
is that they isolate a small section of DNA that is near the gene, and
then use it as a probe to see if the chromosome has the gene.  If the
probe doesn't bind, it means that the gene is not present.

I wouldn't trust it.  It's like the "random number" function in BASIC.
It's not really random, it's psuedo-random.  That is, it takes a seed 
number and then generates a sequence of "random" numbers.  The sequence
isn't really random, it's just that it's hard to figure out what the
sequence will be.  That means that if you know two consecutive numbers
in the sequence, you can figure out the seed number.  Then, you can
figure out all the numbers in the sequence.  That means that your
sequence of "random" numbers is predictable.

Well, as long as you don't have a quantum computer, there is a
practical limit to the size of keys you can break by brute force.
I don't think 80 bits is sufficient.  A 128-bit key can easily
be broken by brute force, if the key is poorly choosen.  A 128-bit
key is just about right for a key that is choosen at random.
A 192-bit key would be much better...

If you have a quantum computer, then all bets are off.  It would
be possible to break 128-bit RSA in a few moments.  So, if you
have a supercomputer, you should use 256-bit keys.  If you have
a quantum computer, you should use 640-bit keys.

1) The original article was written back in 1982, when the IBM-PC

The footprints are preserved in the regolith.  I'm not sure what the
current theory is about how long they'll last, but I think it's a long
time.  The rocks are preserved in the sense that they are not changed,
but there's evidence that they are eroded by micrometeorites, so they
may not last as long as you might think.  There's a good picture showing
the erosion on one of the Surveyor landers in, I think, the August
issue of "Sky and Telescope", that shows how the surface of the lander
has been eroded.  There may be a similar picture in the Apollo Lunar
Surface Journal, which is available on the web.

The landers themselves will probably last longer than the footprints,
simply because they are made of heavier materials.

Jim

I'd rather not get into a debate on the merits of the sanctions
against Iraq.  I'll just say that there are many people who do not
believe that the sanctions are having the intended effect of
punishing Saddam Hussein, and that they are causing much suffering
to the ordinary people of Iraq.

As for the Iraqis "invading" Kuwait, I believe that this is how
many Iraqis viewed the situation.  I've heard that the Iraqis
believe that Kuwait was part of Iraq which was taken by the British.
They weren't invading, they were "liberating" their rightful land.
Of course, this is how the Israelis view the situation in the
occupied territories, and many other examples could be found.

I'm not defending this point of view, but I think it is helpful to
understand it.  If we want to prevent similar situations from
arising in the future, then we need to do more than simply protect
the state of Kuwait.  We need to find a way to resolve these
conflicts - and there are many of them - peacefully.

> You seem to be saying that the purpose of the second ammendment was to
> allow the state to keep guns.  Why would the state need a constitutional
> ammendment to do that?  Any state can raise a militia in the absence of
> an ammendment.  I don't believe that the second ammendment was intended
> to protect the state's right to keep arms, but rather the people's right
> to keep arms.  I don't see how you can justify a right for the state
> that is not also possessed by the people.

Not at all.  The state does not need constitutional authority to be armed,
it has that authority inherent in the concept of the state.  The second
amendment simply states that this authority is not to be infringed.  The
word "people" is used in the second amendment because it is the people
who comprise the militia.  The word "militia" is used in the same context
as "right" in that it is a right of the people, not the state.  In fact,
the second amendment is a limitation on the state, not a grant of
authority.  The state has inherent authority, the people have inherent
rights.

The reason I mentioned the Simon study is that it is one of the few 
double-blind studies of biofeedback in the treatment of hypertension.  

However, it's a study of stress management, not biofeedback.  The
details of the experiment are given in the paper: 

    Stress management training for essential hypertension: a controlled
    comparison.  Stress Medicine, 1987, 3, 251-263.

The way the experiment was done, the experimental group got biofeedback
plus relaxation training.  The results showed a reduction of 5 mm Hg in
systolic blood pressure and 3 mm Hg in diastolic blood pressure.  Note
that this reduction is in the same ballpark as the reduction that can be
obtained using salt restriction (see my earlier posting).  Also, this
reduction is only about 1/3 of the reduction that can be obtained using
medication.

The control group was given placebo training, consisting of a 
supportive discussion group.  The results were a reduction of 4 mm Hg in
systolic blood pressure and 2 mm Hg in diastolic blood pressure.  In
other words, the placebo group got almost as much reduction as the group
that got the biofeedback.  So the biofeedback did not appear to have any
significant effect above and beyond that obtained through the placebo
training.

I'm a little confused about what you want to do.  I'm not clear on
the relationship between the 2-D and 3-D models.  I'm assuming that
the 2-D model has a world coordinate system, and you're trying to
get it to match the 3-D model coordinate system (as opposed to the
screen coordinate system).  If that's true, then you need to find
the transformation that maps 3-D world coordinates to 2-D world
coordinates.  This is composed of the perspective transformation,
the viewport transformation, and the rotation/scaling/translation
transformation.

The perspective transformation is a 4-D to 4-D transformation that
can be expressed as a 4x4 matrix.  The first three elements of the
source and destination vectors are the x, y, and z coordinates in
world coordinate system.  The fourth element is the scaling factor.
The viewport transformation is a 2-D to 2-D transformation that can
be expressed as a 2x2 matrix.  The first element of the source and
destination vectors is the x coordinate in the 2-D world coordinate
system.  The second element is the y coordinate in the 2-D world
coordinate system.  The rotation/scaling/translation transformation
is a 2-D to 2-D transformation that can be expressed as a 2x2 matrix.
The first element of the source and destination vectors is the x
coordinate in the 2-D screen coordinate system.  The second element
is the y coordinate in the 2-D screen coordinate system.

The transformation that you want is the inverse of the product of
the perspective, viewport, and rotation/scaling/translation
transformations.

>How does one power a 12V DC fan using a 120V AC power supply?

You don't.  You have to have the same voltage available to power the fan
as it requires.  If the fan is rated at 12 volts, you must have 12 volts
AC or DC to power it.  If you put 120 volts on the fan, it would probably
be burned up in a second.

Your only choice is to find a power supply that will provide the required
12 volts.  There are many available.  Radio Shack has them for only a few
dollars.  You can also build your own power supply, but it is a bit
complicated.

If you have a power supply and do not know if it will power the fan, I
would advise you to take the power supply and the fan to someone who has
knowledge of electronics to determine the proper use of the power supply
and the fan.  If you do not have the knowledge to make sure the power
supply will work properly with the fan, you could do serious damage to the
fan and the power supply, as well as yourself.

Mike

> system board a reset signal when an IRIM is installed.  If the jumper
> is not installed, the system board will not recognize the 486

I'd just like to add a few points to Jay's answer:
1. If your motherboard has a jumper labeled "system speed", make sure it
is set to 16 MHz.  The motherboard must be set to 16 MHz to make the
486DX2-66 OverDrive processor operate at 33 MHz.
2. If the motherboard has a jumper labeled "CPU", make sure it is set to
"386".
3. The 486DX2 OverDrive processor has a jumper labeled "J1". If you are
using the 486DX2-66 OverDrive processor, the jumper should be
installed.  If you are using the 486DX2-50 OverDrive processor, the
jumper should be removed.

Regards,

    My point was that the DC-X is not a replacement for the Shuttle
    or a Delta rocket.  It is an experiment to test some new ideas.
    As a test vehicle, it is cheap and small.  The operational
    vehicle that may result from the DC-X will be bigger, though
    not as big as the Shuttle.  It will be able to go into orbit,
    but not to the moon.  It will be able to carry a small payload,
    but not a large satellite.  It will be able to carry 1-2 people

    the Delta rocket does.  The difference is that the DC-X is
    re-usable.  If it works, it will be cheaper to launch a payload
    with the DC-X than with an expendable rocket.
    So, if you want to launch a satellite, then you should use a
    Delta rocket.  If you want to send people to the space station,
    launch the space station, or launch a space telescope, then
    you should use the Shuttle.  If you want to go to the moon or
    Mars or an asteroid, then you need to build a whole new vehicle.

> This is a problem?  I thought the whole idea was to make a circuit
> that burned up!

Not exactly.  The idea is to make a circuit that draws a lot of current
and burns up, _but only when the power is turned on_.  The hard part
is not to draw any current when the power is turned off.  It's bad
enough if you have to replace the fuse or reset the circuit breaker
each time you trip over the power cord, but it's really bad if you
have to replace the fuse or reset the breaker each time you turn
the power off and on.  IOW, you have to use a fuse or circuit breaker
that is larger than the normal operating current, but smaller than
the current that would be drawn if the circuit was on continuously.

> I've got to design a circuit with a single 8-bit EPROM that will
> decode 3 digits BCD (3x4pins) and show 3 digits on a 7-segment
> display. I have a 2764 and a 2732 EPROM available. Of course I can
> decode the digits with a PAL, but I want to do it with the EPROM.
> Can anyone help me with this?
> Thanks in advance.

How about this:  Use the BCD digits as the address for the EPROM.  Use
the 8 output bits to drive the segments directly.  Use the 3 digits to
address one of 1000 locations in the EPROM.  You will have to do this
with a 2764.  A 2732 will not work because you need more than 8 address
lines.  The 2764 has 13, which will work. You will have 3 unused address
lines.  You can ground or leave these open.  I believe a 2764 is the
largest EPROM you can use for this purpose.

I don't know if you are aware of the controversy surrounding the
removal of the pituitary gland in the treatment of breast cancer.
There is a preliminary report in the Nov. 1992 issue of the Journal
of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism (Vol. 75, No. 5, p. 1324)
that suggests that the pituitary gland may be a source of
estrogen production in postmenopausal women.  This is only a
preliminary finding and requires further investigation.

What this means is that even if your estrogen production is
suppressed by the removal of the pituitary gland, you may still
have estrogen produced elsewhere, such as the fat cells in your
body.  Therefore, it is unclear whether the removal of the
pituitary gland will have any benefit in the treatment of breast
cancer.

It's a lot easier than it sounds.  There's only two things to worry about:
1.  The two hooks that go into the holes in the frame can be forced
     outward.  The best way to do this is to use a small chisel between
     the hook and the frame and tap with a hammer.  You should see what
     I'm talking about when you take the front bumper off.  It's not
     hard to do, but a little hard to describe.  As soon as you get the
     front bumper off, you'll see what I mean.

2.  The second thing to worry about is that the old bumper is on there
     tight and you may have to break it loose.  Just be careful not to
     break the headlight buckets.  I did this with a crowbar and a
     2x4.  I stuck the crowbar between the bumper and the headlight
     bucket, and the 2x4 between the bumper and the headlight bucket
     (to protect the bucket), and just worked the crowbar back and
     forth, alternating between the two sides.  The bumper will come
     loose.  You can also do this from underneath.  You'll see what I
     mean when you get the front bumper off.

Once you get the old bumper off, installation of the new one is a snap.
You will need new bumper mounting bolts, though.  The old ones were
stretched when the old bumper was put on.

The best thing to do is to take the bumper to a body shop and have them
paint it before you put it on.  It's a lot easier to do then when it's
off the car.  I don't know what body shops are like in your area, but
around here they'll paint the bumper for around $100-$150.  (I live in
the Los Angeles area.)  I would have done it myself, but there was no
way that I was going to spend that much on paint for one bumper.  I
think that the body shop bought the paint for about $50, so they are
making some money, but not too much.

I did the installation myself and it took me about 2-3 hours total.  I
hope this helps.  Good luck!

>either.

That's a very good point.  You can't always assume that the details
of the encryption algorithm have been kept secret (which is another
reason why I don't like the "security through obscurity" idea).

I think that's the point he's trying to make: that the number of
keys -- and the amount of work needed to decrypt -- is much larger
than the number of possible algorithms.  Given some ciphertext,
you can try each possible algorithm in turn, trying each key.
That's a lot simpler than trying every possible algorithm, then
every key for each algorithm.

Of course, this is a gross simplification.  First, there are
probably a lot of "equivalent" algorithms -- the same basic
algorithm with a few parameter tweaks.  Second, there are
probably a lot of "obviously bad" algorithms -- they have
obvious weaknesses, or they're too simple, or they're too
complicated, or whatever.  So there may not be that many
"reasonable" algorithms to try -- although I have no idea
what a "reasonable" estimate of that number might be.

>...

>My understanding is that the key size is about the same as
>the size of the algorithm (assuming a fixed size algorithm).
>So if you can find the algorithm, the key is probably not
>much harder to find.

That depends on the algorithm.  DES, for example, has a 56-bit
key, and (if I remember correctly) an algorithm that can be
expressed in about 1000 bits.

>...

>I guess the only way to settle this is to ask the
>experts.  What do they say?  Is it much harder to
>find the key or the algorithm?  Is it even
>possible to find the algorithm (without knowing
>the key)?

If you have a lot of ciphertext, it should be possible to find
the algorithm.  It may not be possible to find the key, though
-- that depends on the algorithm and the amount of ciphertext
you have.

I work at a teaching hospital that does a lot of EP studies and ablations.  I
have only seen one ablation procedure performed on an outpatient basis.  It
was an unsuccesful ablation attempt at a V-tach focus.  We have had some
patients who have had EP studies and ablations on the same day, but they are
admitted after the procedure.  This is primarily for safety reasons, but
also because most patients are very uncomfortable after the procedure.  I
also know that many of our patients who have these procedures previously had
a pacemaker or defibrillator implanted, so they are not candidates for
outpatient procedures.  I am not aware of any centers that perform EP
studies and ablations on an outpatient basis.  I suspect that the
complications and adverse reactions are too great to attempt these
procedures on an outpatient basis.

>physical therapy to help the problem.  Does anyone know of any
>other treatments?  Has anyone had success with PT for tennis elbow?

This is for chronic tennis elbow.  The treatment is 2 fold.  First
you have to get rid of the inflammation in the lateral epicondyle,
and that may take a couple of injections.  Once the inflammation is
gone, your friend should start doing some specific exercises (I have
a handout that I use for this, but I don't have it with me at home),
which strengthens the wrist extensors, which are the muscles involved.
You can probably get an idea of what the exercises are by going to
a gym and playing around with the wrist curl machines.  The problem
is that most of these machines work the wrist flexors, so you have
to go at it backwards.  The other thing to keep in mind is that
the exercises should be started out slowly and progressed carefully
to avoid reinjury.  As long as your friend is doing the exercises
properly, he should be able to do them gradually, and just as gradually
the pain should go away.  There are some other things that can be
done, but they depend on the particular person and the particular
situation.  Hope this helps (and I hope I haven't forgotten anything
important).

If you saw any flashes of light or floaters, you need to get to an eye
doctor as soon as possible.  I don't know what a "detached retina" is,
but I do know that a torn or detached retina is a very serious condition.
My doctor says that if you see flashes of light or floaters, even if they
go away, the retina may have a tear or may be part way detached.  If this
is the case, then it could completely detach at any time, and then you
lose all vision in that eye.  Even if it doesn't, the retina may be
attached to the back of the eye, but it may get wrinkled or have a bad
connection, and you lose much of your vision.  My doctor said that
if you are in the middle of a flash of light or floaters and you get
to a hospital right away, they can give you a steroid shot to reduce
the swelling and save the retina.  If you wait until the episode is
over, then it may be too late.  Apparently, the retina is very fragile
and it doesn't take much to tear it.  I have no idea what a detached
retina is, but if you had a torn or detached retina, and you didn't
see an eye doctor, then you need to see one right away.  My doctor
also said that tears in the retina are more common in young people
than in old people, and that it is rare to have a detached retina
from old age, but that a detached retina from old age is more serious
than one that is torn or detached from some other cause, such as an
accident or injury.  I hope that helps.  Good luck.

One way is to use the unique decoding property of a good hash such as
MD5.  One can use the hash to generate a pseudo-random number that
selects a byte position in the file.  Then use the byte at that position
as the key to another hash.  The resulting key is then used as a key
to encrypt the file.  A MAC is generated and stored with the file.
The MAC is checked after the file is decrypted.  This technique is
independent of the encryption algorithm used.  It can also be used
to generate keys for public key encryption algorithms.  Of course,
you still have to get the key to the recipient.

I would point out that the DSV does not require much in the way of
general computing power.  The signature generation and verification
algorithms are quite simple even for a field device like a smartcard
(even a slow 8 biter like the Motorola 6805).  In fact, the DSV is
well suited for field applications where one wants to have a
tamper-proof signature on messages sent to and possibly from a
device.  The key space for a 512 bit modulus is 2^120 which makes a
brute force attack virtually impossible.  The DSV is an excellent
solution for many problems.

I have been using the following procedure for encrypting data files and
e-mails for a couple of years now:

1. I use PGP to encrypt the file using a conventional encryption algorithm
   (I use IDEA in 64-bit CFB mode) using a random session key.

2. I use RSA to encrypt the session key using the recipient's public key.

3. I use the "uuencode" utility to do a 7-bit encoding of the encrypted
   file and the encrypted session key.

4. I use PGP to do a 7-bit ASCII armor on the encoded data.

5. I send the resulting file as an e-mail message.

6. The recipient reverses the process using the applicable PGP decryption
   functions and the "uudecode" utility.

I have never had to do anything special to accommodate filenames or file
extensions.  I just encrypt the whole file with its name, and e-mail the
file.

The only thing the recipient has to do differently is to save the PGP
output in a file of the same name as the original file.  The recipient
must also tell PGP not to "strip" the armor so that the PGP output
contains the uuencode information.  This is done by using the "-a" option
to PGP.

I do the same thing with e-mail messages, except that I don't do the
uuencode step.  I just apply the PGP ASCII armor to the encrypted text.

Chris Hibbert

> I just saw a reply about that... I am also trying to design a circuit
> to use for remote control of my computer.  I need to use a regular
> remote control, such as you would use to control your TV or VCR.  I
> want to be able to program the computer to respond to the various
> remote control commands.

I've been mulling over a similar idea for a while, and I'm pretty
sure that I can work something out for it.  The problem with trying
to use a normal remote control is that most of them put out a code
that is a function of the time, not the keys.  These are called
rolling code remotes, and the idea is that they will not be easily
cracked by a hacker trying to get into a car or alarm system.  The
problem with making a remote control for your computer is that
you need a remote that will repeat the code when you press the
button.  A rolling code remote will send a totally different code
every time you press the button, and that makes it very difficult
to decipher the code.

The best solution that I have come up with is to use a learning
remote.  These remotes have a button that you press while the
remote is in a "learn" mode, and it will learn the code from the
remote that you want to duplicate.  After you have saved the codes
to the buttons that you want to use, you can then just press the
buttons to send a matching code.  I have seen these remotes at
Radio Shack, and they are pretty cheap.  If you have any problems
with them, post a message, and I'll see what I can do.

A test for HIV isn't that expensive, and the results are as reliable as
any lab test. 

The question is not whether you have the virus but what your risk
exposure is.  If you have been sexually active with multiple partners
or IV drug users, or shared needles or syringes, or had blood transfusions
or blood products (factor VIII or IX for hemophiliacs), or had a
kidney transplant or artificial insemination between 1978 and 1985,
or if your sex partner had any of these risk factors, you may be at
increased risk.  Otherwise, you probably are at very low risk.

The test is not 100% accurate (no test is), so a negative result
doesn't guarantee you don't have the virus.  However, a positive result
is highly reliable and means you probably carry the virus.  If you have
the virus, you can transmit it to others, even if you have no symptoms
yourself, but you may not develop AIDS for several years or ever.

The best advice is to avoid those risk behaviors that can transmit
the virus.  If you have been engaging in high risk behavior, you should
consider getting tested.  It is confidential, and your insurance company
or employer cannot find out about it.  Call your local health department
or AIDS hotline for information on where to get tested.

in each region of the grid.  Depending on how small you make the grid
your results may be better or worse. This is a pretty simple technique
and should work in realtime for any type of image.

first frequency component to calculate contrast.  This is more work and
probably not worth the effort.

It's caused by dark colored fabric from clothing rubbing off on the leather.

about dye transfer when I had my BMW's seats re-dyed.  The seats were
originally black and the shop used red dye to spruce up the seats.  Since
the original black dye was still there, the red dye didn't stick to the
leather.  After a week of use, the seats had turned purple (red dye on top
of black dye).  The shop had to fully sand down to the original leather
and then re-dye the seats.

Anyway, I would try a leather cleaner like Lexol.  If that doesn't work,
you'll have to get the seats re-dyed.

The problem is not that he is not getting enough protein, but that the
proteins he is getting are not complete.  Even though grains and other
plant foods have lots of protein, they lack certain essential amino
acids.  Combine grains with beans and you have a complete protein food
source.  This combination is the staple of many vegetarian diets.

The problem with this diet is that you are not getting any vitamin B12,
which is essential for brain development.  This vitamin is only found in
animal products.  This is why some vegetarians don't eat animal products
other than milk and cheese.  This is also why some vegetarians get
mental problems.  I have seen a few cases of this.  This is also why
some people do not recommend a strict vegetarian diet for children,

Most people are not aware of this problem.  They think that since the
Buddha ate like this, it must be good.  The problem is that most
vegetarians have not been eating this way all their lives, and so they
have stored up enough of these vitamins in their livers to keep them
healthy for a few years.  But if you were to raise your child on such a
diet, you would see a problem fairly quickly.

For people who are young and healthy, eating a vegetarian diet for a
while is an excellent way to cleanse the body of toxins.  But it is not
a healthy diet for long term use.

>I'm looking for some information (and eventually software) for the 
>generation of prime numbers.  I have seen several articles in the 
>past that describe algorithms for generating large primes, but I 
>have not made an effort to collect them.  Could someone point me to 
>the most recent or best algorithm available.
>
>Thanks,
>
>Joe

I think I recall a paper by Peter Montgomery called something like
"Modular Multiplication Without Trial Division" published in the
Spring 1992 or so issue of the journal of cryptology (but I'm not
sure).  This adds a few tricks to the usual "generate a random number
and try to prove it's prime" method that can help speed up prime
generation.  Also, I think Len Adelmann and/or others have published
some refinements of the Rabin-Miller procedure (the most commonly
used probabilistic primality test) that improve its efficiency
somewhat.

There's also a method called "Lenstra's Elliptic Curve Method" that
can be used to factor a number, which can be used to prove primality
(see below).  This is more complex than Rabin-Miller, but it's
useful for very large numbers that are difficult to test using
Rabin-Miller.  I don't know if anyone has published a paper on how
to use Lenstra's method only for primality testing.  If you want
to learn about complex cryptologic algorithms, a good book is "Handbook
of Applied Cryptography" by Menezes, van Oorschot, and Vanstone. 
It's got a lot of stuff about these sorts of things, and it's cheap
about $40. I'm not an expert on these things, so don't trust anything I say. :-) The "generate a random number and try to prove it's prime" method is: 1) Pick a random number n. The number of digits in n is the "key length". 2) Run some probabilistic primality tests on n. Examples are Solovay-Strassen and Rabin-Miller. These tests will either say "n is definitely composite" or "n is probably prime". Run the test multiple times. The more tests you run, the more sure you are that n is prime if it passes the tests. 3) If n is probably prime, then run some deterministic primality tests on it. Examples are Pollard Rho, Pollard p-1, and Lenstra's Elliptic Curve Method. This will either say "n is composite" or "I couldn't factor it". If n is large, then the deterministic tests may not be able to factor it, in which case you can't prove it's prime. If it's small (say under 34 digits), then you can use a method that can prove it's prime, such as the APRCL primality test. If n is too large to prove it's prime, you can use it anyway if you're confident enough that it will be very hard for anyone else to factor it. If n is composite, then go to step 1. This gives you a prime number n. The next thing you need is a primitive root modulo n. This is a number g such that: 1) g is between 1 and n-1, and 2) for every number x between 1 and n-1, there is a number y such that: g^y = x (mod n). This means that every number between 1 and n-1 is equal to a power of g (mod n). If you pick a primitive root g, then you can publish n and g as public keys, and keep secret the number x. The number y = g^x (mod n) can also be published, since it is very hard for anyone else to figure out x given just g and y. The number x is the private key. This is the basis of some public key cryptosystems, such as the El Gamal signature scheme and the Diffie-Hellman key exchange protocol.

I am not sure if you have seen this, but it was interesting to me.  I have

in hearing what the results of these tests were, if you had them.

>> other is running NT.  Both use the same printer, which is

>> sharing turned on on both computers, and I can print from the NT
>> computer to the printer connected to the Windows 3.1 machine,
>> but I can't print from the Windows 3.1 computer to the printer
>> connected to the NT machine.  Has anyone encountered this problem
>> before?  Does anyone have a solution to this problem?

> Windows 3.1 will only print to networked printers on a Windows NT
> server if the server is running the NetBEUI protocol.

> I would expect the same to be true for the other way round.  Make
> sure the NT server is running NetBEUI.

I'm not sure if this will help or not, but I had the same problem with a
Win3.1 machine connected to a NetWare server.  The problem was that the
Win3.1 machine was running Microsoft's client software, which is very
different from Novell's client software, and not configured to support
Microsoft's broadcast name resolution protocol (NetBEUI).

If you are running 3.1 with the Microsoft client, try adding the line:

NETBUI=0

to the [network] section of the SYSTEM.INI file on your Windows 3.1
machine.  It will force your 3.1 client to use Microsoft's broadcast name
resolution protocol and should fix the printer problem.

If you are asking the question "Is it possible to create a cryptographic
scheme in which you can take a message, make a small change, and still
have the resulting encrypted message look like it's only a slightly
changed version of the original encrypted message", then the answer is no.
Such a system would be very easy to break.  It would merely be a matter
of trying different changes to the original plaintext message and seeing
which ones were reflected in the ciphertext message.  For example, one
might change the first letter of the plaintext message, see if this was
reflected in the ciphertext message, and then repeat the process for
the second letter, third letter, etc. until one had broken the ciphertext.

Who said anything about the Big Bang?  We are talking about cosmic
inflation, and this cosmology does not predict a Big Bang, but rather
a Big Bounce.  The universe expands and then contracts, over and over
again.  The implication is that the universe is eternal.  And even
if the universe is finite in age, it doesn't matter, because time
began at the beginning of this particular cycle of expansion and
contraction.  There was no time before the Big Bang, just as there is
no space north of the North Pole.

----------------
John Gribbin, "In Search of the Big Bang", pg. 374:

    One fascinating implication of the new observations [of
    cosmic inflation] concerns the beginning of the universe.
    There is a popular, but mistaken, impression that the
    theory of inflation implies a beginning to the universe.
    Inflation itself does not say anything about the beginning
    of the universe.  It is a scenario that can be patched
    onto any pre-existing cosmology, provided that the
    cosmology starts in a state of extreme density, which is
    required for inflation to get started.  In many versions
    of the Big Bang theory, there is a definite beginning to
    time, since the equations of general relativity break
    down when you extrapolate mathematical models of the
    universe back to the point where everything was crushed
    together.  Inflation makes it possible to avoid this
    difficulty.  In the inflationary universe, the expansion
    of the universe takes place in a kind of cosmic
    breathing, with periods of expansion alternating with
    periods of contraction.  Although the theory has been
    worked out in detail only for the expanding phase, it
    seems likely that a contracting phase would precede the
    inflation, and, perhaps, an indefinite number of
    expanding and contracting phases would precede our own
    expanding phase.  In that case, there would be no
    beginning to time, and no moment of creation.

    This idea is not just science fiction.  The equations of
    general relativity allow for it, and they are the only
    equations we have for describing the overall structure
    of the universe.  The idea is also consistent with the
    idea of cosmic inflation, provided that each phase of
    contraction is followed by a new phase of inflation.
    It is even possible to have a universe which contracts
    to a small, but finite, size, and then bounces outward
    into a new phase of expansion.  The equations of
    general relativity do not allow the universe to shrink
    to a size smaller than about 10 to the minus 33
    centimeters across, a size known as the Planck length.
    At that size, quantum effects become important and
    prevent the universe from shrinking any further.
    In effect, quantum uncertainty acts like the air in a
    tennis ball, preventing the universe from being
    crushed flat.  And just as the air in a tennis ball
    bounces back when the ball is squeezed, so the universe
    bounces back into a new phase of expansion after it has
    reached its minimum size.

----------------

In other words, there was no beginning to the universe.  Time is
eternal.  At least, that is what the current cosmology predicts.
Although it is possible to interpret the evidence to support the
idea of a beginning, it is not necessary.  The universe could
quite well be eternal.

In an eternal universe, there is no need for a god to create
it.  The universe is quite capable of creating itself.  The
universe existed before it was created.  The universe was its
own mother.  Or perhaps, the universe is the child of another
universe.  The idea of a universe birthing another universe is
not without precedent.  There is evidence to suggest that black
holes may be the birthplaces of new universes.  You see, our own
universe may be the child of a black hole in another universe.
We may be living inside a black hole right now.  We cannot see
outside the black hole, because the horizon of a black hole
is a one-way boundary, but we can speculate about what is on the
other side.  Perhaps the other side is another universe.  There
is no way to know for sure.  We can only make guesses based on
what we can observe.  And what we can observe is that our
universe is a big black hole.

> If the voltage difference is less than 100 volts, you can use a
> neon lamp to indicate the voltage with just a 1 megohm resistor in
> series.  Use an NE-2 or its equivalent. The resistance is just
> enough to prevent the neon from conducting during the negative
> cycle of the AC line and to limit the current when it conducts
> during the positive cycle.  The neon will flash at 60 hertz and
> give a very dim light.  If you want to make it bright, use a
> bridge rectifier and a 1000 UF capacitor (100 volt or greater) in
> parallel with the neon.  The capacitor will charge up to a level
> that will give enough current through the neon to make it bright.
> You can use two neons in series with a 1 meg resistor and no
> bridge rectifier if you want to make a line voltage indicator
> without the bridge rectifier.  The two neons will flash in
> opposite phase so each will be on half the time.

I don't know what you mean by "pre-suppositionalist".  I have not heard
the term before.  I am a Christian and also a philosopher.  It is
irrelevant to the discussion of the logical consistency of the Christian
World View whether or not I believe in it.  I, as well as many other
Christians, can and do appreciate the logical validity of the Christian
World View.  That is why I am a Christian.  I believe that the Christian
World View is true because it is logically consistent, internally and
externally.

If you can show me how the Christian World View is logically inconsistent,
I would be most grateful.  I am not aware of any one who has done this.
Those who claim that the Christian World View is inconsistent usually
commit the "Straw Man" fallacy by misrepresenting Christianity and then
showing that what they have misrepresented is inconsistent.  Other times
they commit the "Faulty Analogy" fallacy by taking an analogy which is
only isomorphic to a certain extent.  The usual Christian response is to
point out the fallacy and then show that it is not Christianity, but the
misrepresentation of Christianity which is inconsistent.  I have never
seen this response refuted.  I have seen many attempts, but no one has
ever been able to overcome the fallaciousness of their argument.

If you wish to claim that Christianity is logically inconsistent, you
will have to show a logically inconsistent set of propositions that are
essential to the Christian World View.  I will then show you that the
propositions are not essential to the Christian World View, or that the
propositions are consistent.

As a matter of fact, I would be willing to wager with you that you are
not able to show that the Christian World View is logically inconsistent.
Everything that you say about Christianity will either be a misrepresentation
of Christianity or it will not be logically inconsistent.  If you wish to
accept my wager, let me know.

Those who proclaim that science is the only valid way of gaining knowledge
are making a dogmatic statement, not a scientific one.  If they try to
back up their dogmatic statement with a scientific argument, they are
committing a logical fallacy.

If a scientist were to say, "I have never experienced any phenomena which
could not be explained scientifically," that would be a valid scientific
statement.  But if he said, "I have never experienced any phenomena which
could not be explained scientifically, therefore nothing exists which cannot
be explained scientifically," that would be a logical fallacy.

I can say that I have never experienced a dog talking, but that doesn't
mean that a dog has never talked.

> 2. I want to encrypt and decrypt some data (e.g. credit card number or
>    an email) but I don't want to have to enter a password each time I
>    encrypt/decrypt.  How can I do this?

> 3. I want to encrypt a file and send it to a friend who will decrypt it
>    using the same algorithm.  How can my friend decrypt the file without
>    having the original key I used to encrypt it?
>    decrypt it without having the original key I used to encrypt it?

If you want to do all this securely, you need to use a combination of
symmetric and asymmetric encryption.  Depending on which of these you
want to do (probably all of them), you need to use the following:

1. You can't do this securely.  You can use a one-way hash function
   and store the hash value, but if you can encrypt your password
   and decrypt it later, so can someone else.

2. You can't do this securely.

3. This is the function of public key cryptography.  Your friend
   generates a key pair, and you encrypt the file using his public
   key.  He decrypts it using his private key.

I'm assuming that you don't want to have to enter a password to do
any of these operations.  In response to the above, you could use
a password to protect the encryption key, but then you'd have to
enter the password each time you encrypt/decrypt.

Methylphenidate is a central nervous system stimulant and an appetite
suppressant.  Methylphenidate is used in the treatment of attention
deficit disorders with and without hyperactivity, narcolepsy and as an
adjunct to anti-depressants.  Methylphenidate is also used for its
anorectic effects.

Methylphenidate is available in oral tablets and sustained release tablets.
It is also available in solution for injection.

The most common side effects associated with methylphenidate are nervousness
and insomnia.  Other side effects include dizziness, headache, dyskinesia,
drowsiness, anorexia, nausea, dry mouth, weight loss, palpitations, increased
heart rate, increased blood pressure, tachycardia, rashes and hypersensitivity
reactions.

Methylphenidate is contraindicated in patients with glaucoma, marked anxiety,
tics, or a family history or diagnosis of Tourette's syndrome.  Methylphenidate
is contraindicated during treatment with monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors and
should also not be administered for 14 days after discontinuation of MAO
inhibitor therapy.  Methylphenidate is contraindicated in patients with a known
hypersensitivity or idiosyncrasy to the sympathomimetic amines.

I'm not sure about the data on the shuttle's flight.  I don't know about
the 3,000,000 BTU/hr at 1,000 ft/s.  The shuttle certainly does not have
that kind of thrust capability, and the original statement said that the
shuttle was "flying" at 1,000 ft/s.  I doubt that the shuttle could stay
up at that speed.  As for the "3,000,000 BTU/hr" specification, I'm not
sure what the poster meant by that.  I'll assume that this was the
required heat rejection rate of the shuttle, and that it is at least
approximately correct.  That would correspond to about 900 kW of power. 
I don't know how much power a shuttle (or any particular shuttle
component) needs, so I don't know how reasonable this is.  Perhaps a
shuttle engineer on the net could comment on this.

At any rate, this heat rejection rate would be an average over the entire
mission.  This is not very useful for the present discussion, because the
heat rejection rate would vary widely over the course of the mission. 
It's possible that the heat rejection rate could get up to 900 kW
temporarily during the ascent, but you would probably need to average
over several minutes to do this.  The requirements at the moment of
reentry would be much smaller.  The shuttle is now in a gliding descent,
and would not require much power to maintain its systems.  And since
reentry only lasts a few minutes, the total heat load from the shuttle
systems would be small compared to the heat load from reentry.  So it is
reasonable to assume that the radiative heat load from the shuttle is
negligible during reentry.  If the poster can come up with evidence that
the shuttle does need a lot of power during reentry, then we can
recalculate the heat load from the shuttle's systems and see if it
changes the conclusion.  But I think it's safe to neglect it for now.

So, let's reexamine the problem of a 90 ton vehicle reentering the
atmosphere at 7000 m/s.  The heat load of 220 kW/m^2 is still correct
(assuming the radiative heat load from the shuttle is negligible).  The
surface area of the shuttle (assuming a flat plate) is

A = (90 tons)(1000 kg/ton)(1 m^2/100 kg) = 900 m^2.

The total heat load is then approximately

Q = (220 kW/m^2)(900 m^2) = 200 MW.

This is a heat load of 2 MW/ton.  The heat load per unit area is not
constant, but varies with position on the shuttle.  The heat load is
highest at the nose and leading edges of the shuttle, and falls off
toward the rear.  But this is an average, and is probably a reasonable
approximation to the actual heat load near the belly of the shuttle.

The shuttle would have to reject 200 MW of heat during the entire descent
(about 20 minutes).  The total heat load is then

Q = (200 MW)(20 min)(60 s/min) = 240 GJ.

This is the total heat load for the entire descent.  We can compare this
to the energy of the shuttle as it reenters the atmosphere.  The shuttle
has a mass of 90 tons, and a velocity of 7000 m/s.  The kinetic energy is
then

KE = (1/2)mv^2 = (1/2)(90 tons)(1000 kg/ton)(7000 m/s)^2 = 2200 GJ.

So the total heat load is about 11% of the kinetic energy of the shuttle. 
This is not a lot of energy to dissipate.  It would be interesting to
know how much heat the shuttle's tiles can absorb before they are damaged
or destroyed.  I don't know the mass of the shuttle's tiles, but I would
guess it's about 10 tons.  (It's a lot, but the shuttle is a big vehicle. 
And those tiles are not light.)  The specific heat of the tiles is about
837 J/kg-K.  (This was determined experimentally at JPL, and is probably
accurate to within 10%.)  If all of the heat load went into heating the
tiles, their temperature would rise by

dT = Q/(mc) = (240 GJ)/(837 J/kg-K)(10 tons)(1000 kg/ton) = 29 K

No - it's much worse, because the signature is on a SHA-1 digest of the
data.  SHA-1 has no known vulnerability, and the birthday attack isn't
really practical.  So if you get a message with a valid signature, you
know it was originated by the person with the private key.

The problem is the opposite: if you get a message without a valid
signature, then the person with the private key can always claim that
the message was forged, and you have no way to prove otherwise.

Since the message is sent in plaintext, you can't even prove that the
sender sent the message.  You'd have to have some kind of physical
evidence, such as a videotape of the sender typing the message.

I asked for clarification from the author of the original message, and
he said that the message must be sent in plaintext to be compatible
with the mime standard.  I don't know if this is true or not.  Anyone
know of a mime standard for encrypted mail?

>How come if you got a cut and you put hydrogen peroxide on it and your
>lungs hurt?  I had a cut on my leg and put hydrogen peroxide on it and
>my lungs hurt.  I didn't think it was suppose to do that.  What's wrong
>with me?

You have a really fast metabolism, or you had a deep cut and you
did a lot of scrubbing, or you have some kind of allergy, or someone
put something else in the peroxide bottle, or you are making this
up as a joke.

Peroxide is a very weak oxidizing agent.  It is a good disinfectant
because the oxidizing action will kill most bacteria.  It is not
that corrosive to human skin, although it will kill skin cells just
like it does bacteria.  That is why it is used as a gargle or mouthwash
to kill the bacteria in your mouth.  It is also why it is used to
clean wounds.  The "foaming" action is actually the formation of
oxygen gas as the peroxide breaks down into oxygen and water.  The
oxygen gas "scrubs" the wound, removing dirt and bacteria.

The action of peroxide in breaking down into water and oxygen is
very easy to see.  Just take a small piece of liver (raw, not
cooked) and pour a little peroxide on it.  You will get a lot of
foaming.  This is a chemical reaction between the peroxide and the
cellular material (enzymes) in the liver.  The enzymes in your skin
will also cause the peroxide to break down into oxygen and water,
but the reaction is much slower than in liver.  When you put
peroxide on a wound, the foaming is a chemical reaction between the
peroxide and the enzymes in the bacteria and the enzymes in the
wound itself.

The peroxide is very unlikely to cause any problems when used as a
mouthwash or to clean wounds.  The only hazard I can think of is
that if you put a very large quantity of peroxide on a wound, the
foaming action would be quite violent, and it would create a lot of
oxygen gas.  If the wound was in your lungs and the gas bubbled up
through your throat, you would get an oxygen bubble in your mouth.
If you were foolish enough to inhale, you might get a bubble of
oxygen in your lungs, and that would be very uncomfortable.  That
is a very unlikely situation.

It is possible to buy peroxide in concentrations of 3% (household
peroxide), 6%, 30%, and 90%.  The 3% solution is safe to use on
skin, and is the only concentration usually found in a drug store.
The stronger solutions should only be used in industrial
applications.  If you were to drink a solution of more than 6%
peroxide, it would be very dangerous.  When it contacted the
enzymes in your stomach, it would break down to water and oxygen,
and the oxygen would create a lot of foaming in your stomach.  This
would be very painful.

I think the most likely explanation is that you were just imagining
that your lungs hurt.  If you really are sure you felt something,
you should see a doctor.  Maybe you have an allergy to peroxide.

> This is an area that has been studied quite a bit.  In effect, the
> "training" effect of vaccines works because the immune system is
> "trained" by exposure to the vaccine to respond to similar but not
> identical antigens.  So the vaccine is not identical to the AIDS
> virus, but it looks enough like it to generate a response in the
> immune system.

> The question is how much different the virus and vaccine can be
> and still work.  This is a lot more complex than it might seem at
> first, because the immune system is capable of making a response
> to almost anything you can imagine, and the only limits are how
> much of a response, how long the response lasts, and how fast the
> response is mounted.  So the virus and vaccine don't have to be
> identical in every way, just enough to get a response that will
> be able to fight off the virus.

> And the response isn't necessarily even to the virus itself.
> Most of the time the virus is hidden away inside a cell, and
> the immune system never gets to "see" it.  Instead, the immune
> system sees bits and pieces of the virus that the cell presents
> to it, and from these bits and pieces the immune system tries to
> generate a response that will kill the virus.

> For some viruses, vaccines are pretty simple to make.  For
> example, the polio vaccine is a killed virus that is pretty much
> identical to the real thing.  Another example is the flu vaccine,
> which is a mixture of several different flu viruses that caused
> problems in the past.  Each year's vaccine is different from the
> previous year's, but it always contains the viruses that caused
> the most problems in the previous year.

> For other viruses, vaccines are much more difficult to make.
> The AIDS virus is an example of this.  The AIDS virus hides inside
> cells, and the only bits and pieces that the immune system sees
> are the envelope proteins.  These proteins are not enough to
> generate a response that will kill the virus, so a vaccine based
> on these proteins will not work.

> The AIDS virus is also a lot more variable than the flu virus.
> The flu virus changes a little bit every year, but the AIDS virus
> changes a lot more than that.  The AIDS virus is also a lot more
> complicated than the flu virus.  The flu virus has a few proteins
> that it uses to infect cells, but the AIDS virus has a lot more
> proteins that it uses to infect cells, and these proteins are
> much more variable than the flu virus proteins.

> So a vaccine for the AIDS virus would have to be a lot more
> complex than a vaccine for the flu virus.  It would have to
> include a lot more proteins, and these proteins would have to be

I was writing up a reponse for this when Steven answered.  The Merck Index
is the best source.  Biotin is a simple 5 ring structure.  Cyanocobalamin
is a 4 ring structure with a dimethyl benzene ring, a pyrrole ring, and a
pyrazole ring joined by carbons to an imidazole ring (with a methyl group
on the 2 position) with a cyanide group on the imidazole nitrogen.  The
imidazole ring is also bonded to a 5-carbon ring with an amine group
attached (also at the 2 position) on the 5th carbon.  Folic acid is a
pteridine trione bonded to a p-amino benzoic acid, which is in turn bonded
to an L-glutamic acid.  Pantothenic acid is a 5-C ring with a methyl group
on the 1 position, a carboxylic acid on the 2 position, a carboxylic acid
on the 4 position, and a hydroxyl group on the 3 position that is bonded
to a 2,4-dihydroxy-3,3-dimethyl butanoic acid.  Riboflavin is a
7,8-dimethyl benzene ring with an alcohol group on the 6 position, a
carboxylic acid on the 4 position, and a methyl group on the 5 position.
The 10 position is bonded to a D-ribityl group.  The D-ribityl group is a
5-carbon ring with a hydroxyl group on the 1, 2, 3, and 4 positions.  The
1 position is also bonded to a 6,7-dimethyl isoalloxazine ring.  Thiamine
is a 5-C ring with a methyl group on the 3 position and a hydroxyl group
on the 4 position.  The 5 position is bonded to a 4-methyl thiazole ring.
The 2 position is bonded to a 2-hydroxy ethyl group.  Pyridoxine is a
2-methyl pyridine ring with a hydroxyl group on the 3 position, a
hydroxyl-methyl group on the 4 position, and a hydroxyl group on the 5
position.

Just in case someone else has problems with the CUDA, I thought I'd 
describe our problems and how we overcame them.

We had problems with the external gates not working properly.  We would 
get a readout of 00000000, but the gates would not open.  This only 
happened when we tried to operate the board in an external mode.  

The problem was that when the board is in an external mode, the external 
inputs would override the internal inputs.  We had neglected to tie the 
external inputs to ground.  The solution was to wire all of the external 
inputs to ground.

We had problems with the internal inputs not working properly.  We would 
get a readout of 00000000, but the gates would not open.  This only 
happened when we tried to operate the board in an internal mode.  We had 
neglected to tie the external inputs to ground, and the floating inputs 
were overriding the internal inputs.  The solution was to tie the 
external inputs to ground.

We had problems with the board not working at all.  The readout would 
read 00000000, and the gates would not open, regardless of which input 
mode the board was in.  This problem was solved by reseating the board.

We had problems with the board working, but not consistently.  The readout 
would read 00000000, and the gates would not open, regardless of which 
input mode the board was in.  This problem was solved by replacing the 
board.

We had problems with the gates working intermittently.  The readout would

mode the board was in.  This problem was solved by replacing the gates.

I've been in the same boat. I'm writing a bitmap "paint" program. I've been using
the BltToDC() function from the toolbox. I was having the same problems you are. I
tried using CopyBits() and everything worked smoothly. It's a bit harder to use,
but it's worth it if you want speed. If your screen is set to the same mode as your
offscreen buffer (ie 8-bit or 16-bit), then copying the pixmaps is a breeze. I hope
that helps.

Here are some test vectors for the RC5 encryption algorithm, as described
in the article "The RC5 Encryption Algorithm" by Ronald L. Rivest, which
appeared in the proceedings of the 1995 Fast Software Encryption
workshop.  All test vectors use the standard ROR and ROL functions.

The vectors are of the form:

	<# of rounds> <key> <plaintext> <ciphertext>

where all values are given as 64-bit ASCII hex strings.  For example,
the 32-bit key "0x01234567" is represented by the 64-bit ASCII hex
string "3031323334353637".

>It is my understanding that the temperature of the jet exhaust is
>extremely high.  Why can't the water be heated up to produce steam
>that will get rid of the water altogether?

The exhaust is very hot, but the temperature of the gases at the
nozzle exit is limited by the throat temperature.  For a rocket
engine, the throat temperature is limited by the melting point of the
nozzle material.  If you increase the chamber temperature and pressure
to increase thrust, you have to widen the throat area proportionately
to keep the throat temperature constant.  The result is that the
nozzle exit temperature is almost independent of the chamber pressure.

He's right.  There is a substantial body of evidence that they exist,
and that they make a complete sphere around the sun.  Of course the
mass out there is so small that it's not worth much of anything.  The
total mass of the Oort cloud is about 1/1000th the mass of the sun (or
about 1/3rd the mass of Jupiter).  Its density is about 1/1000th of an
atom per cubic centimeter - and that's in the densest parts of the
cloud.  That's a density so small that it's hard to imagine.  If you
had a cubic meter of the stuff, I think you'd have a hard time finding
any atoms in it - there would be about 1 atom per cubic centimeter.

There is of course some evidence that the cloud extends past 1 light
year.  Long period comets have been observed that orbit out to about 2
light years from the sun.  The evidence for the cloud is quite solid,
but the evidence for how far it extends is mostly based on the
assumption that long period comets are from the Oort cloud, so the
cloud isn't well characterized.

The reason it's so sparsely populated is that the solar wind is
strong enough to ionize the outermost layer of molecules on the surface
of the comets.  The solar wind then blows the outermost layer of the
comet away.  If you've seen pictures of the tail of a comet, you've
seen what's happening to the comet.  The tail is the outer layer of the
comet being blown away by the solar wind.

So, as the comet travels towards the sun, it loses a layer.  The comet
has to be pretty well made to survive the trip, but the ones that do
make it are the ones we see.  With each trip, the comet is smaller
until finally it's completely gone.  A comet can make about 1000 trips
before it's completely gone, and it's probably more likely to be
captured by a planet or the sun than to survive 1000 trips.  So, if
you're wondering why there aren't more comets, that's the reason.

The cloud has an interesting property.  It's so thin that when a comet
is ejected it has a high probability of never encountering another
comet.  When it's ejected, it goes out into a very large region of
space.  If the comet is gravitationally bound to the sun (in an orbit)
and it gets out to about 2 light years, it's very hard for it to get
back in.  It's got to have a close encounter with another comet to
change it's orbit.  But if it's out there, the odds are against it
having an encounter with another comet.  The chance of it encountering
a star is greater (there's a whole lot more stars than comets, even in
the Oort cloud).  So, once the comet is out there, it's gone.  It's
gone from our solar system (and won't be back for millions of years if
ever), and it's gone from the universe (because it will soon be in
another solar system - or not in any solar system).

The Oort cloud is a bit of a mystery.  That's because it's very hard to
observe.  The only way to observe it is to wait for a comet to come by
and then observe the comet.  The comet is so small and so far away that
it's hard to observe, but if you can catch one, you can find out a lot
about the cloud.

I think that's about all I can think of.  I hope this helps.

> inactivated vaccines of less efficacy than the live vaccines?  If
> so, why are they still used?

I believe that the inactivated vaccines are less efficacious than
the live ones.  The primary reason for still using them is the
belief that they are safer.  There are occasional reports of
children who develop polio after receiving the live vaccine, and
some parents are concerned about this.  The other reason for using
inactivated vaccines is that they can be made in the absence of a
culture of poliovirus.  The live vaccine must be made in the
presence of growing poliovirus, presenting some risk of infection
to laboratory workers.

A recent post by Bob W6SDO stated:
> While the 2.4 GHz output of a microwave oven is about 1 watt, the
> power density is fairly high because it is confined to a small
> space.

I don't think that this is correct.  The power density in the oven is
not high: it is low.  The oven is a resonant cavity and the power
density is quite low at the center of the cavity and rises to a maximum
at the walls.  The reason is that the cavity is excited with a
relatively low power and these resonant modes of the cavity are quite
broadband and hence store little energy.  The cavity is designed so
that the walls are reflective, which means that the E field is maximum
at the walls.  The power density is proportional to E^2, so it is
maximum at the walls.  The food is placed near the center of the cavity
where the power density is low.  The maximum power density is at the
corners of the oven where the fields are maximum and are in phase.

The following is an abstract from the 1994 American Society of Clinical
Oncology meeting held May 14-17 in Dallas, Texas.  This abstract was
submitted by the listed authors, and was not reviewed or selected by the
American Society of Clinical Oncology.  The content of this article does
not necessarily reflect the policies, views, or attitudes of the American
Society of Clinical Oncology, unless so stated.

JOURNAL:  Proc Ann Meet Am Soc Clin Oncol 13: A1301, 1994

TITLE:  Prolonged survival of patients with metastatic breast cancer
receiving paclitaxel as second or third line therapy:  A phase II study

AUTHORS:  T. Sahmoud; S. Nabholtz; K. Gelmon; S. Norris; J. Fisher; M.
Stewart; C. Steward; M. Pater; D. Gertler; C. Trudeau; M. Pauzner;
M. Latreille; M. Dion; J. Stewart

AFFILIATION:  McGill University, Montreal, PQ, Canada

BACKGROUND:  The taxoids are a new class of chemotherapeutic agents
which have activity in a wide variety of malignancies.  This
multicenter trial was designed to evaluate the efficacy of paclitaxel
in patients with metastatic breast cancer previously treated with
anthracycline-containing regimens.

PATIENTS AND METHODS:  Patients were required to have histologically
confirmed breast cancer, to have received no more than one prior
chemotherapy regimen for metastatic disease and to have measurable or
evaluable disease.  Patients were treated with paclitaxel 200 mg/m2 IV
over 3 hours every 21 days.  The median age of the 30 patients treated
was 52 years (range 36-76).  The majority of patients had visceral
disease (n=22) and 24 patients had received two or more prior
regimens.

RESULTS:  As of September 1993, 29 patients were assessable for
response.  The overall response rate was 52% (8 CR, 8 PR) with a
median duration of response of 12 months.  The median time to
progression was 8 months.  The median survival time is 13 months (95%
CI:  9-17 months).  Grade 3 and 4 toxicity was 33% and 7%,
respectively.  Grade 3 leukopenia occurred in 17% of patients and
grade 4 in 3% of patients.  There were 2 episodes of grade 3 and 1
episode of grade 4 thrombocytopenia.  Grade 3 and 4 infections were
observed in 2 patients.  Grade 3 and 4 neurotoxicity occurred in 2 and
1 patients, respectively.  Other grade 3 and 4 toxicities were rare.

CONCLUSION:  These preliminary results show that paclitaxel, as
second or third line therapy, is effective in patients with metastatic
breast cancer with an acceptable toxicity profile.  The median
survival of 13 months compares favorably with other second line
regimens.

I don't know if it's been mentioned, but a number of SGI's GL
implementations have a bug in the polygon offset code.  Specifically,
the offset is not applied correctly when the width of a line segment is
not equal to one pixel.  In particular, if you use glLineWidth to make
"fat" lines, they will not be correctly offset from the corresponding
polygon edges.

The most important thing is to keep the patient comfortable.  If the patient
is uncomfortable, the parents are uncomfortable, and the nurses are
uncomfortable.  Therefore, the patients are usually loaded up with Ativan
and Morphine.  It's very common for patients to be on a morphine drip and
have boluses of ativan available.  The morphine is titrated according to
the pain level of the patient.  We are always monitoring the pain level of
the patient, and we have a pain scale we use.

Another thing we do, is we listen to the parents.  They know their child
better than the nurses, and we find out what has been effective for them
in the past, and use that, too.

Tony, you are kidding, right?  Weight has a lot to do with it.  If you
don't believe me, you should compare a 2 seater sports car with a 4 seater
luxury car.  If you need more convincing, compare a full sized pickup with
a compact pickup.  As far as self-cleaning, I am not sure what you mean.
I have a car with a manual transmission and I have an automatic.  Both of
them have the same clutch assembly (with the exception of the clutch
pedal).  But the manual transmission has a clutch disc which is driven by
the engine.  The automatic has a torque converter and the clutch disc
drives the torque converter.  The torque converter is filled with fluid
which acts as a coupling between the engine and the clutch disc.  I don't
think I have ever heard of a clutch assembly that is self-cleaning.

Otherwise, I think your ideas are right on the money.  Automatics should
be less efficient because of the fluid coupling which is not 100%
efficient.  But with the same size engine, a car with an automatic
transmission should be able to tow a heavier load because the torque
converter is a very low gear which helps to get the load moving.  With a
manual transmission, you would have to use a lower gear to get the load
moving.  Then you would have to shift to a higher gear (one that is
equivalent to the torque converter) and that would be very difficult to
do without stalling the engine.

I think that the only advantage that a manual transmission has is the
greater control that you have over the car.  For example, when driving in
snowy conditions, you have to be careful not to spin your wheels.  With a
manual transmission, you can use a higher gear to reduce the amount of
torque to the wheels.  This is especially important when you are starting
from a stop.  With an automatic transmission, you don't have this control.
The automatic always tries to use the lowest gear possible.  This may
cause the wheels to spin excessively.  The automatic transmission also
causes the car to lunge forward when you try to start from a stop.  This
is because the torque converter is a very low gear.  This is not a very
big problem in normal driving, but it can be a problem in snowy
conditions.

The term "solar flare" is generic. It's used to describe any sudden 
increase in brightness of the Sun in a particular wavelength, such as 
radio waves or X-rays. A solar flare in the X-ray spectrum will be quite 
different from a radio solar flare, because they are produced by 
different mechanisms. Keep in mind that the Sun is not just a big ball 
of gas. It's a big ball of gas with some very complicated and poorly 
understood physics going on in it. 

I don't know much about solar flares, but I know that solar flares are 
caused by magnetic fields, and that the Sun's magnetic field is very 
complex. I'm sure that there are many different mechanisms which can 
cause a flare in a particular wavelength. For example, the Sun's 
magnetic field can cause particles to be accelerated to very high speeds. 
When these particles hit some other part of the Sun, they can emit a 
burst of X-rays. I imagine that this is what happens when you get an 
X-ray flare. But it's pretty obvious that an X-ray flare is going to 
behave differently from a radio flare, because different mechanisms are 
involved. 

I would be very interested in hearing more about this. I'm sure that 
there are many different types of solar flares, and that they are 
produced by many different mechanisms. I have no idea if the different 
types of flares are related in any way, or if they are completely 
independent events. I don't know how much is known about solar flares, 
but I'm sure that there is a lot that isn't known.

Phil

That's a good question, and I don't have a good answer for it. 
The only thing I can think of is to make the committee 
choose a fixed number of parameters of the function, and 
choose them independently of the other parameters. 
That is, if you have a 512-bit hash function, and you want to 
choose 128 bits of it, then you can choose 128 bits as 16 
128-bit hash functions on 32-bit blocks. 
Then the committee has to choose the 128 bits of the function 
independently. But I'm not sure that this is really any better. 
It doesn't solve the problem of the committee having to choose 
128 bits, but it does help to ensure that the committee 
isn't just making up the bits as it goes. 
It also helps to ensure that the committee doesn't have to 
choose the bits in a way that makes it easy for the NSA to 
make the function less secure. 
But I don't know if this really helps. 
It's still not clear to me whether or not it's a good idea. 
I'm not sure that it's any better than choosing the bits 
independently.

the original question as I recall it was whether one could
simulate a shadow in a painting.  I think the answer is no,
one can not.  Even if one could, the resulting image wouldn't
look like a painting, it would look like a simulation of a
painting.  The best one could hope for would be to make a piece
of art that looks like a painting.

If you have a shadow in an image, the first thing that the
viewer is going to do is look for the object that is casting it.
If that object is not there, the viewer will be confused and
irritated.  I think it is also important to know where the
source of light is in a painting.  If you can't find the source,
you will be irritated.

I don't think that there is anything wrong with using computers
to produce art.  Computers are great tools.  But you don't use
a hammer to pound in a screw.

I don't know what kind of test your doctor is using, but the most
accurate way to measure iron is to measure the saturation of iron
transporting protein called transferrin.  A transferrin saturation
below 25% means that iron absorption is not optimal.  25 to 35%
saturation is good for normal adults.  35 to 45% is good for
pregnant women and children.  45 to 55% saturation is considered
high normal.  55 to 100% saturation is considered high.

Hope this helps,

Harold A. Davis, Jr.

> All I know is that I had to turn the volume up on my monitor.
> I was getting the "click" sound which is the same as the
> "click" from the speaker.  Now after the monitor went "pop"
> the "click" is gone.  I can turn the sound all the way down
> and turn the monitor up all the way and still cannot hear the
> "click".  I still have the "click" from the internal speaker
> though.  I use the sound card and monitor for my sound.
> I use the internal speaker for my errors.

The "click" you were hearing in your monitor was the sound of an arc
inside the monitor's power supply.  The "pop" you heard was what happens
when the arc gets big enough to melt something.

I'd guess that your monitor developed a short in it's power supply that
caused it to arc.  The arcing caused the volume from the monitor to rise,
and it probably caused some damage to the monitor's audio section as well.
In fact, the short may have occured in the audio section of the monitor,
but I wouldn't count on that.  The arcing should have tripped a circuit
breaker or blown a fuse somewhere, too.  If it didn't, then you could have
a fire brewing in your monitor.  Turn it off and have it repaired.

Mark, I would suggest the following:

1) Try to see if there is any way you can work with your advisor to
get the project done.  Talk to your advisor and try to explain what is
going on.  If you can rekindle some enthusiasm, you may be able to
finish up in a reasonable amount of time.

2) If you are unable to work with your advisor, then you may want to
try to find a new advisor.  Go to other professors and ask if they
would be willing to take you on.  Obviously, you will need to have a
research topic that is acceptable to the new advisor.  The advisor
will need to be aware that you have not been able to get along with
your current advisor.  You will have to be careful in how you approach
this so that your current advisor does not look too bad.  You may
even want to say something like "due to circumstances beyond my
control...." to get the advisor to know that you are not a flake.

3) If your advisor is a flake, then find someone else.  Life is too
short to spend it trying to please someone who is impossible to please.
If you can get your old advisor to write a nice letter to your new
advisor, then even better.

4) If you can't come to an agreement with your advisor, then you are
in a pickle.  You could consider leaving the program and starting over
someplace else.  If you can get the old advisor to not write nasty
things about you, then you can probably get into another program
without too much trouble.  However, you will have to explain why you
didn't finish the program at the previous place.

In sum, I would suggest that you try to work out something with your
advisor first.  If you can't, then try to find a new advisor.  If
that doesn't work, then you may want to consider leaving the program
and starting over.

Yes it does matter, but probably not much in this case.

First, make sure that the max input spec of the amp is not exceeded.  The
output of the scope is low impedance, so I would guess that the max input
of the amp is somewhere around 20 volts or so.  In this case, you can set
the scope output to 20 volts/div, and then select the x10 probe.  Then
each division on the scope will represent 2 volts.  The amp input will
then be at its max, giving you the best resolution for your measurements.

Note that the x10 probe has a 9 meg resistance, so the input impedance
of the scope will be 9 meg in parallel with 1 meg (9 * 1 / (9 + 1) ). 
If the amp input impedance is 10 kilohms, then the voltage attenuation
at the amp input will be 10e3 / (10e3 + 9e6 + 1e6) = 0.999 or 99.9%. 
This is negligible.

A 1x probe will have a 10 meg resistance, giving a total input impedance
of 10 meg in parallel with 1 meg = 0.909 meg.  The voltage attenuation
at the amp input will be 10e3 / (10e3 + 0.909e6) = 0.01097 or 1.097%. 
This is also negligible, but is a greater error than that of the 10x
probe.

If you use a 1x probe, the max output of the scope will also be 20 volts.
So, if you keep the scope voltage/div setting at the same value, you will
have less resolution on the scope display.  This is also true for any
vertical amplifier applied to the signal before the scope input.

Bob Masta

You know, for all the complaints about the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo
programs that they were "junk" and "just a stunt" and "only got us to
the Moon" and "did nothing for us", I'd just like to note that, in the
scope of NASA's history, the Shuttle is really not that old.  I mean, it
has only been flying for 15 years, and it has already flown more missions
than the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo programs put together, and has
already carried more people into space than all those programs put
together, and has already spent more time in space than all those
programs put together.  And it has more than doubled the time, missions
and people of the Soyuz program.

The Shuttle is the most advanced spacecraft in the world, and is the
basis of all the manned spacecraft projects in the world, including the
Soviet/Russian programs.  It is the most used spacecraft in history.  It
is the only spacecraft to have a program of regular missions to orbit
and back.  It is the only spacecraft to have flown people from 5
different countries (the US, Canada, Germany, France and Saudi Arabia),
and people from every continent except Antarctica.  It is the only
spacecraft to have a reusable crew cabin.  It is the only spacecraft
that can launch and return cargo to and from orbit.  It is the only
spacecraft to have operated in orbit for more than two weeks.  It is
the only spacecraft to have carried a crew of eight.  It is the only
spacecraft to have carried a woman into orbit.  It is the only
spacecraft to have carried a person of African descent into orbit.  It
is the only spacecraft to have carried a person of Asian descent into
orbit.  It is the only spacecraft to have carried a person of Middle
Eastern descent into orbit.  It is the only spacecraft to have carried
a person of Native American descent into orbit.  It is the only
spacecraft to have carried a person of Latin American descent into
orbit.  It is the only spacecraft to have carried a person of Pacific
Islander descent into orbit.

When you look at it this way, it seems that the Shuttle program has
already done a lot for us, and, in fact, is still doing a lot for us.
More, in fact, than many realize.  I've heard people say that we should
just scrap it and do something different.  Well, there is no better
alternative, and won't be for at least another 20 years.  The Shuttle is
still the best way for us to get to and from space.
